title: Orange roof, blue cupola
label: Brand gallery
lede: The building was the advertisement. The roof tiles were a particular orange chosen to catch a motorist’s eye, and a New England cupola sat on top.[^1] The photographs and postcards below are free-licensed or public domain; the drawings are ours.

archive.caption: Howard Johnson’s, Nashua, New Hampshire. Linen postcard by Tichnor Brothers of Boston.
archive.alt: Postcard of a white restaurant with an orange roof
archive.credit: Tichnor Brothers, publisher; Boston Public Library collection, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Howard_Johnson%27s,_Nashua,_N.H_(77857).jpg). Public domain.

archive.caption: “The Midway on America’s Super Highway”: the Howard Johnson restaurant at the Midway plaza of the Pennsylvania Turnpike.
archive.alt: Postcard of a stone turnpike service plaza
archive.credit: Published by Howard Johnson Publishing Department, Bedford, Pa.; printed by Tichnor Bros., via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:The_midway_on_America%27s_Super_Highway,_Howard_Johnson_Restaurant_(79695).jpg). Public domain.

archive.caption: Entrance to a full-service Howard Johnson’s restaurant in Pennsylvania.
archive.alt: Restaurant entrance with an orange roof and teal spire
archive.credit: Photo: Christopher Ziemnowicz (CZmarlin), via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Howard_Johnsons_restaurant_1999_PA_entrance.jpg). Public domain.

archive.caption: The Lake George, New York restaurant, then one of the last three.
archive.alt: A low restaurant building with an orange roof and a blue spire beside a parking lot
archive.credit: Photo: Jennifer Rafieyan, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Howard_Johnson%27s_in_Lake_George.jpg), CC BY 2.0.

blocks.title: The same roof, about seventy years apart

before.label: c. 1930–1945
before.caption: Nashua, New Hampshire, when the chain was spreading along New England’s highways.[^27]
before.alt: Postcard of the Nashua Howard Johnson’s

after.caption: Lake George, New York, fifteen years before it became the last to close.[^27][^14]

drawings.title: Twenty-eight flavors.
drawings.caption: The business began with a high-butterfat ice cream in 1925.[^1] Original illustration.

drawings.title: The clam plate.
drawings.caption: Fried clams were a specialty of the first restaurant in 1929 and were still on the menu in Bangor in 2016.[^1][^11] Original illustration.

drawings.title: Next exit.
drawings.caption: Highway sites produced 85% of the business in the 1970s.[^1] Original illustration.

disclaimer: Colours are approximations chosen by eye from the photographs above, not official specifications. Howard Johnson and Howard Johnson’s are trademarks of their owner.
